title: Signal-to-silence benchmark: one-pager
content:
Summary:
This one-pager summarizes a focused benchmark that quantifies the tradeoffs between end-to-end latency and unit cost when reducing 'silence' (idle gaps between emitted tokens) in streaming generation. The goal: give product and runtime teams a compact view of how three production-relevant serving configurations behave on short multi-token generation workloads and surface pragmatic levers for product SLAs.

Motivation:
- Customers building chat/assistant flows care more about time-to-first-meaningful-token and perceived responsiveness than raw throughput.
- Many cost optimizations (large batching, tiling) increase idle gaps between token emissions — improving cost but hurting perceived latency.
- We need a simple signal that ties together token-level emission regularity (signal-to-silence), observed percentiles, and $/token for realistic session lengths.

Benchmark setup (condensed):
- Model: open-compat 13B equivalence (substituted with internal profile).
- Hardware: 1x V100-equivalent GPU serving runtime (profiled on our staging Dedicated cluster).
- Workload: 10k trace-replay sessions, each session requests a 32-token continuation after a 16-token prompt; sessions drawn from real chat traces (mixed short-turn, question/answer, code snippets).
- Concurrency: 1k concurrent session arrivals (poisson arrival, bursty coefficient 1.8).
- Measurements: end-to-end response latency (first-token and full-response), p50/p90/p99 of token-emit intervals, tokens/sec (system-level throughput), $/1M tokens estimated based on internal cost model.
- Configs compared:
  * aggressive-batching (throughput-first): large window batching, opportunistic tiling, minimal prefetch
  * streaming-low-latency (responsiveness-first): small-batch prefetch, priority fast-path, immediate flush on first token
  * hybrid-windowed (middle): short windows + KV-prefetch heuristics, conservative batching for tail smoothing

Key metric: signal-to-silence ratio (S/S) = total time emitting tokens / total active session time. Higher means fewer idle gaps observed by the client.

Results (compact):
ASCII table (end-to-end latency for a 32-token response; dollars per 1M tokens):

Config                 | p50 (ms) | p90 (ms) | p99 (ms) | tokens/sec | S/S ratio | $/1M tokens
-----------------------|----------|----------|----------|------------|-----------|------------
aggressive-batching    | 200      | 480      | 1400     | 12500      | 0.34      | $88
streaming-low-latency  | 75       | 160      | 420      | 3500       | 0.92      | $142
hybrid-windowed       | 110      | 240      | 720      | 7200       | 0.67      | $105

Interpretation:
- Aggressive-batching delivers the best $/token and highest throughput but the lowest S/S ratio — long idle stretches appear between token emissions; p99 latency is high and user-perceived responsiveness suffers.
- Streaming-low-latency markedly improves p50/p90 and S/S (tokens are emitted steadily) but costs ~60% more per token on this workload due to lower packing efficiency and more frequent kernel invocations.
- Hybrid-windowed gives a middle ground: meaningful S/S improvement over aggressive batching with moderate cost uplift. It smooths p99 relative to aggressive while retaining better packing efficiency than pure streaming.

Mini-chart: token-emit cadence (example session, normalized):
- aggressive-batching : [==-----==------=====-----] (bursty emits with wide silence)
- streaming-low-latency : [============================] (dense, low-silence emission)
- hybrid-windowed : [====---=====---=======---==] (partial smoothing)

Recommendations (short):
1) For consumer-facing chat where perceived latency matters, default route should be hybrid-windowed with optional escalation to streaming-low-latency for premium tier or first-N-turns. (Owner: Maya Li)
2) Optimize prefetch heuristics to increase S/S for hybrid mode with <10% cost delta: focus on hot KV-cache warm paths and lightweight lookahead for likely next tokens. (Owner: runtime team)
3) Expose a developer-facing knob: response-pace-profile {throughput|balanced|responsive} with clear expected p90/p99 and $/1M tokens in the Console. (Owner: console team)
4) Instrument a client-visible S/S metric and show it in per-route dashboards to help customers choose tradeoffs. (Owner: observability)

Caveats and notes:
- Numbers are stage-cluster approximations; absolute $/token will change on different GPU classes. Use the relative deltas for decisioning.
- The workload favors short multi-token bursts; very long continuations change amortization and will narrow relative cost gaps.
- p99 in aggressive mode is sensitive to microburst arrival patterns; runtime admission shaping reduces p99 but increases visible silence further.

Next steps / experiments (ordered):
- Run a follow-up with NVL8-class profiles + mixed sequence lengths (1k sessions, longer tails) to validate cost delta at scale. (Diego)
- Prototype a hybrid prefetch policy that increases S/S by selectively pinning KV shards for hot sessions; measure S/S uplift vs CPU overhead. (Runtime)
- Add a Console tooltip that translates S/S into user-facing wording (\"steady streaming\" vs \"bursty emission\") and add to docs. (Console + Docs)

Appendix: raw summary numbers (median of 5 runs)
- aggressive-batching: median tokens/sec 12,450 | mean token-emit gap 28ms emission bursts / 80ms idle gaps | infra cost model $88 per 1M tokens
- streaming-low-latency: median tokens/sec 3,520 | mean token-emit gap 3ms steady | infra cost model $142 per 1M tokens
- hybrid-windowed: median tokens/sec 7,170 | mean token-emit gap 8ms steady with small pauses | infra cost model $105 per 1M tokens

If you want this converted into a two-slide customer-facing narrative (short charts + TL;DR), I can draft one. For the next internal run I recommend we parameterize prompt lengths and test 8B/70B variants to check frugal vs heavy models.
